concepts.name: Loose piece
concepts.wording: A piece that is undefended but not currently attacked. Not a loss yet — the raw material of a future tactic.
cautions: Strong players leave pieces loose constantly and correctly, when no forcing move can exploit it.

concepts.name: Weak square

cautions: A weak square covered by a piece is not exploitable while that piece stays; the plan is to trade it off first.
Conceding weak squares is routinely the right price for space, the bishop pair, or a tempo.

cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

concepts.name: Check
concepts.wording: Check: the king is attacked, and the side to move has exactly three ways to answer — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker. Nothing else is legal, which is why a check is the most forcing move there is.

A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.

concept.name: Pawn promotion
concept.wording: Promotion: a pawn arriving on the eighth rank is replaced immediately, as part of the same move, by a piece of its own colour. The choice is free and unlimited — a side may have several queens — and it is not confined to pieces already captured.
cautions: Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.

concepts.wording: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. cautions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.

cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Doubled pawns
concepts.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.

concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concepts.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concepts.name: The bishop pair
concepts.wording: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
cautions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

An advanced square, usually protected by a pawn, that no enemy pawn can attack — so a piece placed there cannot be driven away. Sources disagree on whether an open or half-open file behind it is part of the definition.

concept.name: Outpost
